To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the very old with mild Alzheimer disease (AD) have less abnormal brain morphology and cognition than young-old patients with mild AD, and that this difference is explained by an age-associated decrease in cortical thickness.

(1) in the very old, cognitive and structural brain changes associated with AD may be less salient than in the young-old and may be less severe than expected, given their level of cognitive impairment; (2) this effect may be explained by age-related differences in cortical thickness in HC participants; and (3) the results underscore the importance to interpret neuropsychological test scores and brain measures in reference of the individual's age.
